hitting our $1.2M ARR wasn't about going viral or huge ad spend.

it was boring, tiny site tweaks most people miss.

here are the 8 steps & prompts that boosted your traffic and conversions:

0. Understand the Full System

website optimization isn’t just about changing the design.

it comes down to three stages:

① build a foundation Google and AI can crawl and understand
② attract visitors with useful content
③ use data to turn those visitors into signups and purchases

ranking on Google isn’t enough.

if AI engines can’t understand your content—or visitors land on your site but don’t understand the value—you still won’t get results.

the key is identifying which stage is broken and improving it with a clear goal.

if you want to improve your website or grow your organic traffic, bookmark this.

1. Understand What’s Happening With Data

the first step is making sure you can see what is actually happening.

not guesses. real data.

the two main tools you need are Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console (GSC).

both are free.

GA4 shows what people do after they visit your website:

・which pages get the most traffic
・whether visitors come from Google, social media, or other channels
・whether visitors come from AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity
・which pages lead to signups or purchases

Google Search Console shows how people discover you through Google:

・which keywords your pages appear for
・how many people click from search results
・your average search position
・which articles are gaining or losing rankings

with these two tools, you can separate two very different problems:

“not enough people are visiting”

vs.

“people are visiting, but they aren’t taking action”

connect GA4 and Google Search Console to NoimosAI, and it can analyze the data and suggest what to improve.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to identify the room for improvement:
“Analyze traffic from Google Search and AI search engines using GA4 and GSC, then recommend the pages with the highest improvement potential.”

“Using GSC data, identify articles that have lost rankings and recommend which ones should be rewritten.”

2. Build a Technical Foundation Google and AI Can Understand

you can create the most useful content in your industry.

but if Google and AI can’t properly crawl and understand it, people won’t find it through search results or AI-generated answers.

here’s what to check:

・are your important pages indexed by Google?
・does your sitemap tell crawlers which pages exist?
・is robots.txt accidentally blocking Google or AI crawlers?
・does the site load quickly and work well on mobile?
・are there broken links or layout issues?
・does JSON-LD clearly identify your company, products, and articles?
・does llms.txt organize your most important pages for AI?

robots.txt, sitemaps, and JSON-LD create a shared technical foundation for both traditional search and AI search.

the work that helps Google discover and understand your pages is called technical SEO.

GEO goes one step further by making your content easier for AI engines to understand and use in their answers.

NoimosAI can analyze page speed, site structure, robots.txt, JSON-LD, and other technical issues—then recommend improvements for both search engines and AI.

use this prompt in NoimosAI to optimize your site:
“Audit [Website URL] for search engine and AI readability. Analyze robots.txt, the sitemap, JSON-LD, llms.txt, and page speed, then recommend specific improvements.”

3. Communicate Your Value Above the Fold

visitors decide within seconds whether they want to keep reading.

the first screen they see should answer three questions:

・who is this for?
・what problem does it solve?
・what should I do next?

listing dozens of features won’t help if visitors can’t see why the product matters to them.

for example, describing NoimosAI as “a powerful AI agent” is too abstract.

“delegate your marketing work to AI” makes the outcome much easier to understand.

don’t just describe the product.

show people what changes after they use it.

prompt to find the best messages for your site:
“Analyze the first screen visitors see on [Website URL], then suggest a headline and supporting copy that communicate the value immediately.”

4. Give People a Reason to Trust You and Take Action

interest alone doesn’t create signups.

even when people understand your service, they may still wonder:

“does this actually work?”

“will this work for my company?”

your website needs to answer those questions with evidence.

use things like:

・real product screenshots
・specific use cases
・customer results
・testimonials
・supported integrations
・security information
・pricing and the steps required to get started

don’t add everything just to make the page longer.

choose the proof that addresses the biggest concerns customers have before signing up.

on the NoimosAI website, we show the product, supported services, customer testimonials, and security information before guiding visitors toward getting started.

5. Choose Keywords That Can Generate Revenue

once the foundation is ready, you need to attract the right visitors.

a better website won’t generate results if nobody sees it.

start with the problems your customers are already searching for on Google.

then create articles that solve those problems and introduce your product as one possible solution.

the key: don’t target a keyword just because it has high search volume.

for example, “best AI tools” may get a lot of searches, but it is extremely competitive.

more specific keywords like:

“best AI tools for social media posts”

or:

“best AI tools for competitor analysis”

usually have clearer intent and less competition.

use data from Semrush or similar tools to find keywords that:

・match a real problem your customers have
・have enough search volume to matter
・aren’t dominated by impossible competition
・show comparison, evaluation, or purchase intent

a good keyword doesn’t just generate traffic.

it attracts people who could eventually become customers.

use this prompt to find the best keywords to get visitors:
“Find keywords that customers of [Product or Service] are searching for. Organize them by search volume, ranking difficulty, and search intent.”

6. Create Articles That Rank on Google and Get Understood by AI

once you choose a keyword, analyze the pages already ranking for it.

top-ranking pages reveal what people are expecting to find.

but copying the same information gives people no reason to read your article.

first, analyze the SEO side:

・what topics appear across most top-ranking articles?
・what order makes the information easiest to understand?
・what information is missing?
・what information is outdated?
・where can you add your own experience or data?

then make the structure easy for AI to understand:

・answer one clear question under each heading
・give the direct answer first
・summarize the most important points
・include examples, numbers, and sources
・add an FAQ at the end

don’t write an FAQ that avoids the question.

answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then explain the reasoning and examples.

this makes the article easier for readers to scan and easier for AI to extract useful answers from.

that’s a core part of GEO.

NoimosAI can analyze Google search results, create the article structure, write the content, and include summaries, direct answers, and FAQs designed for both SEO and GEO.

prompt:
“Analyze the top-ranking search results for [Keyword], then create an SEO/GEO-optimized article targeting that keyword.”

7. Use Data to Find What to Improve

publishing a page is not the finish line.

algorithms change. information becomes outdated. customer behavior changes.

you need to keep improving based on what the data tells you.

the same “underperforming page” can have completely different problems:

・high search impressions, but few clicks
　→ the title or description isn’t compelling enough

・high rankings, but little traffic
　→ the keyword may have low search demand

・high traffic, but few signups
　→ the content, CTA, page flow, or trust signals may be weak

・an article used to perform, but rankings dropped
　→ the information may be outdated, or competitors may now offer better content

don’t try to fix every page at once.

identify the cause, then start with the pages where a small improvement could create the biggest result.

prompt to use in NoimosAI:
“Using GSC and GA4, categorize pages into: ① pages that don’t appear in search, ② pages that appear but don’t get clicked, and ③ pages that get traffic but don’t generate signups. Recommend improvements for each.”

8. Compare Before and After, Then Keep Improving

website optimization is never a one-time project.

when you change a title, check the click-through rate.

when you update an article, check its search ranking.

when you change the page structure, check the signup rate.

record every change and compare the numbers before and after.

that’s how you learn which improvements are actually driving results.

here’s what we review every month:

・pages gaining or losing search impressions
・pages gaining or losing traffic from ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other AI services
・pages with low click-through rates
・articles losing rankings
・high-traffic pages that don’t generate signups
・pages with speed issues
・traffic sources generating signups or purchases

we use NoimosAI agents to continuously identify keyword gaps and rewrite underperforming content.

feed these prompts into NoimosAI to find the gap between you and your competitors:
“Every week, identify high-priority keywords that competitors rank for but we don’t, then create one new article idea.”

“Every month, compare the latest 28 days with the previous 28 days. Use search rankings, clicks, and traffic from AI services to identify the article with the highest improvement potential and create a rewrite plan.”

website optimization isn’t about launching a flashy redesign.

it’s about:

・building a system that measures results
・making your value easy to understand
・creating content around real customer problems
・improving continuously based on data

repeat this process, and your website stops being a static company brochure.

it becomes a system that consistently generates customers.

5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

text:
THE DRUG ROUTE INTO INDIA

A fact based investigation from Afghanistan and Pakistan to Punjab, from Myanmar to the Northeast, and from the border to India's streets

The Indian drug problem is often presented as a story about addicts.

That is the wrong place to begin.

The real story begins thousands of kilometres away, in places where opium is cultivated, synthetic drugs are manufactured, armed groups control territory, criminal organisations operate across borders and legitimate trade can be used to conceal illegal cargo.

By the time a packet of heroin reaches a young person in Punjab, or a tablet of methamphetamine reaches a college student in Kerala, the product may already have passed through several countries, several intermediaries, shell businesses, transport networks, financiers and local distributors.

India sits between two of the world's most important illicit drug producing regions.

To the west lies the Golden Crescent, centred historically on Afghanistan and extending through Pakistan and Iran.

To the east lies the Golden Triangle, centred on Myanmar, Laos and Thailand.

India shares a 3,323 kilometre border with Pakistan and a 1,643 kilometre border with Myanmar. It is therefore not simply a destination market. It can also become a transit country. 

And the nature of the threat is changing.

The old image of the Indian drug trade was largely heroin and opium. The newer picture contains methamphetamine, MDMA, LSD, cocaine, synthetic stimulants, pharmaceutical drugs and drugs ordered through encrypted communications and delivered through increasingly sophisticated logistics.

The most important question, therefore, is not whether India has a drug problem.

It does.

The question is what happens when two international drug corridors meet an enormous domestic market.

That is where this story begins.

---

CHAPTER ONE

THE GOLDEN CRESCENT

Afghanistan, Pakistan and the western route into India

For decades Afghanistan has been one of the world's principal sources of illicit opium.

The geography explains part of it. The politics explains another part. Decades of conflict weakened state control over remote areas, while opium provided farmers, traders and armed groups with a highly profitable commodity that could move across borders.

But there is an important fact that is sometimes missed in today's discussion.

Afghanistan's opium economy has changed dramatically since the Taliban announced its ban on poppy cultivation.

UNODC estimates that Afghanistan cultivated approximately 232,000 hectares of opium poppy in 2022. By 2025 that had fallen to approximately 10,200 hectares. Estimated opium production fell to 296 tonnes in 2025, down 32 percent from 2024 and dramatically below the pre ban period. UNODC estimated that the 2025 crop could produce approximately 22 to 34 tonnes of export quality heroin. 

That does not mean the Afghan drug threat disappeared.

Existing stocks remain.

Trafficking networks remain.

Processing and distribution networks remain.

And the trade has increasingly adapted.

The western drug corridor now has several important components.

Afghanistan remains a source of opiates.

Pakistan provides a major geographical corridor between Afghanistan and India.

Iran provides another major trafficking corridor and maritime route.

The Arabian Sea provides access to India's western coast.

The product can then move inland.

This is why the Indian authorities increasingly describe the western drug problem not simply as smuggling, but as an organised transnational network.

UNODC has noted that heroin traditionally entered South Asia through the India Pakistan land border, but that the pattern has changed. Iran became an important departure point for shipments identified by Indian authorities, with a substantial proportion entering India by sea. 

The western route therefore has multiple doors.

The land border is one.

text:
In 2025, an NIA case involving drone delivered explosives and arms resulted in convictions of nine accused. The investigation linked the operation to Pakistan based and Germany based terrorist handlers and the Khalistan Zindabad Force. 

That is why the term narco terrorism has entered India's security vocabulary.

It does not mean every drug smuggler is a terrorist.

It means that where criminal drug networks intersect with terrorist financing, weapons trafficking or terror organisations, the drug trade becomes a national security problem.

---

# CHAPTER FOUR

## THE INDIAN SIDE OF THE NETWORK

The international supplier is only one part of the machine.

Someone has to receive the consignment.

Someone has to store it.

Someone has to transport it.

Someone has to distribute it.

Someone has to collect the money.

Someone has to launder the proceeds.

And someone has to protect the network from detection.

This is where the Indian drug trade becomes more complicated.

The evidence from major investigations points to a layered structure rather than a single organisation.

At the top can be an overseas supplier or handler.

Below that can be an Indian receiver.

Then come transporters and warehouse operators.

Below them are local distributors.

At the bottom are street dealers and users.

The money moves in the opposite direction.

The drugs move down.

The money moves up.

The system can involve legitimate businesses, rented premises, bank accounts, properties and apparently ordinary commercial transactions.

The Mundra investigation exposed the use of shell import companies. The Attari investigation exposed the use of legitimate trade documentation, godowns, Indian entities, bank accounts, property purchases and hawala. 

There is another layer.

Officials themselves can sometimes become compromised.

In April 2025, Punjab Police arrested eight people in a Pakistan backed drug cartel investigation, including a DRI inspector, according to police. The investigation also identified Dubai based hawala operators. 

In another Punjab case in 2025, police arrested a head constable along with three employees of Punjab State Power Corporation Limited in a heroin trafficking investigation. 

These cases do not prove that government agencies as institutions are part of the drug trade.

They prove something more uncomfortable.

A large criminal economy can sometimes penetrate institutions designed to stop it.

That is the difference between corruption being an isolated crime and corruption becoming an enabling component of organised crime.

---

# CHAPTER FIVE

## POLITICS ENTERS THE PICTURE

This is the chapter where facts must be separated from political claims.

There is evidence of individual politicians and political workers becoming accused or arrested in drug related investigations.

There is not evidence sufficient to say that an entire political party is a drug trafficking organisation.

Those are completely different claims.

Punjab provides several examples.

Former Congress MLA Satkar Kaur, who later joined the BJP, was arrested by Punjab Police in October 2024 in a case involving alleged heroin supply. Police said 100 grams of heroin was recovered during a decoy operation. 

In 2025, Shiromani Akali Dal leader and former Punjab minister Bikram Singh Majithia was arrested in a disproportionate assets investigation arising from a drug case. Punjab Vigilance Bureau alleged that more than Rs 540 crore in drug money had been traced in the investigation. The allegations remain matters for the legal process and should not be treated as a conviction merely because an arrest occurred. 

In 2026, an AAP backed village sarpanch in Tarn Taran was arrested by NCB after investigators reported the seizure of 18 kilograms of heroin. 

[3 /n]
_source_value: illegal betting website blocked India police

text:
Another AAP local leader was arrested in Amritsar in 2026 in a case involving 4.3 kilograms of heroin and weapons, according to police reports. 

The pattern is more useful than the party labels.

Different political affiliations have appeared in different cases.

That tells us that the drug economy is not automatically loyal to one ideology.

It is loyal to money.

The same principle applies to the police.

Individual police officers have been arrested in drug cases.

That does not mean Punjab Police is part of the drug trade.

It means any system handling enormous quantities of illegal money is vulnerable to infiltration.

The correct response is therefore not to declare an entire political party, police force or government agency guilty.

The correct response is to follow the money, the communications, the properties, the bank accounts and the chain of custody until the evidence identifies the individuals involved.

That is precisely why financial investigations have become increasingly important.

---

# CHAPTER SIX

## THE SECOND FRONT

### Myanmar and the Golden Triangle

Now move east.

The geography changes.

The problem does not.

Myanmar sits at the centre of the Golden Triangle, historically one of the world's major opium producing regions.

But the Golden Triangle has undergone a major transformation.

Methamphetamine has become increasingly important.

UNODC describes the Golden Triangle as a major hub for both opium and synthetic drug production and says methamphetamine has become the dominant drug in seizure data in the region. Methamphetamine seizures in East and Southeast Asia increased substantially over the past decade. 

The heart of the problem is Shan State.

Remote terrain.

Weak governance.

Long running armed conflict.

Cross border trade.

Criminal networks.

Armed groups.

And enormous profits.

These conditions create an environment in which drug manufacturing and trafficking can survive even when governments conduct enforcement operations.

UNODC has reported that criminal organisations and armed groups in the Golden Triangle sometimes cooperate around illicit economies and that political instability and corruption in Myanmar, particularly in Shan State, have aggravated the problem. 

The important point is that this is not a simple story of one organisation manufacturing drugs.

It is an ecosystem.

Manufacturing networks.

Armed groups.

Traffickers.

Financial operators.

Transporters.

Corrupt intermediaries.

And international criminal organisations.

The exact participants can change.

The business model remains.

---

# CHAPTER SEVEN

## THE DRUGS COMING FROM MYANMAR

The principal concern for India's Northeast is heroin and methamphetamine.

Methamphetamine appears in different forms.

Yaba tablets are methamphetamine based tablets widely trafficked in the region.

Crystal methamphetamine is another form.

The Northeast is especially exposed because India shares a 1,643 kilometre border with Myanmar through Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram. 

The problem is not theoretical.

UNODC has documented the westward movement of methamphetamine from Myanmar into South Asia.

Its 2025 regional synthetic drugs report noted that methamphetamine trafficking flows from Myanmar into northeastern Indian states continued in early 2025. The report also cited a Mizoram seizure of 236.44 kilograms of methamphetamine tablets in May 2025 and a seizure of 30.4 kilograms of methamphetamine tablets in Assam in April 2025. 

Myanmar's own production remains substantial.

UNODC estimated Myanmar's potential opium production at 995 tonnes in 2024. 

But the bigger strategic concern is the synthetic market.

Synthetic drugs do not depend on agricultural land in the same way as opium.

A laboratory can produce enormous quantities.

Production can move.

Precursors can move.

text:
In a residential neighbourhood of Jaipur, coaching centres have been running for years in buildings meant for homes. Students arrive in large numbers, traffic clogs the lanes, and residents complain of noise, parking chaos and the quiet conversion of planned residential zones into commercial hubs.

Recently on 4 August in Loganathan vs, State of T.N case the Supreme Court has now called the situation “not only shocking but also alarming.” From an individual demolition case that began in Chennai, the Court has expanded the proceedings into a pan-India exercise against unauthorised constructions and illegal change of land use. The question is no longer whether the problem exists. It is whether the institutional machinery that allowed it to grow will finally be made to work.

By Nancy Mahavir Sharma

text:
What started as a challenge to demolition proceedings against a G+1 building erected without sanction in Chennai quickly revealed a deeper pattern. The Court observed that such a construction could not have come up unnoticed. It spoke of collusion and connivance of municipal authorities and an “alarming state of affairs.”

Instead of confining itself to one petitioner, the Division Bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R. Mahadevan converted the matter into a continuing supervisory jurisdiction over urban governance across the country. Municipal corporations of state capitals were impleaded. Chief Secretaries of every State and Union Territory were brought on record. An Amicus Curiae was appointed as nodal officer for citizen complaints. Affidavits were demanded, personal appearances ordered, and costs enhanced for non-compliance.

https://t.co/zBrMd8x7Rg

text:
The Court has repeatedly returned to the principles laid down in Rajendra Kumar Barjatya. Unauthorised constructions are not to be encouraged. Violations must be dealt “with iron hands.” Administrative failure cannot become a defence. Completion certificates and utility connections in illegal buildings must be scrutinised. Officials who look away must face departmental consequences. Appellate authorities dealing with demolition and penal orders must dispose of pending matters within defined timelines. These are not new rules. They are the existing law, restated because the existing law has been treated as optional.

Jaipur figures prominently in the latest order. Land earmarked under the Master Plan is alleged to have been put to uses contrary to the sanctioned land use. Land surrendered for planned development has neither been properly utilised nor protected from encroachment. Coaching institutes continue to operate from premises that cause hardship to residents even though the government has constructed dedicated multi-storeyed complexes for their relocation. Those complexes, the Court was told, are reportedly being allotted to other institutions, defeating the very purpose for which they were built. The Jaipur Development Authority has been directed to place on record the corrective measures it has taken, its Commissioner must file a personal affidavit, and pending appellate matters must be decided within two weeks. Any further allotment of the dedicated buildings will remain subject to the final outcome of these proceedings.

1. India Rejects USCIRF's Call for Sanctions on RSS

According to Union Home Minister Amit Shah, eligible refugees from Bangladesh who were forced to leave their country due to religious persecution will be granted citizenship within six months. UPDATE TO ALL MEMBERS ON LOCUM ENGAGEMENT & CASUALIZATION

The leadership of NARD, ably led by the Strategic P-MUS (Garkuwan Matasan Arewa), is pleased to update members on the outcome of the FMoHSW Committee on  Regulation and Casualization of Doctors.

Following extensive consultations, the Committee has developed a National Policy on the Engagement of Locum, aimed at ensuring fair, transparent and non-exploitative engagement of temporary healthcare personnel.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Recruitment & Approval:
   Locum engagement must be based on a clearly identified staffing gap and approved by the appropriate hospital authorities.

2. Contract Duration:
   Initial locum contracts shall not exceed 6 months, with only one additional 6-month renewal permitted. Continuous engagement for 12 months makes the position eligible for permanent appointment.

3. Maximum Work Hours:
   Healthcare personnel shall work a maximum of 48 hours per week, including weekends. Excess hours must be appropriately compensated.

4. Maximum Duty Period:
   No healthcare personnel shall work beyond 24 continuous hours, including call duty.

5. Mandatory Rest:
   
   - Minimum 12 hours between shifts.

   - Mandatory 24-hour post-call rest after weekday and weekend calls.

   - A 1-hour break after 6 hours of continuous work.

6. Call Duty:
   
   - Maximum 2 calls per week.

   - Maximum 1 weekend call per month.

   - Calls must be equitably distributed.

7. Remuneration & Welfare:
Pay rates are standardized in alignment with the government's 
Scheme of Service. Remuneration must be paid monthly without delay, accompanied by monthly 
payslips. 

Locum staff are entitled to all government-approved leaves, public holidays, and occupational insurance coverage.

8. Excess Work Hours:
   Excess hours must be properly documented, monitored and adequately compensated, or appropriately balanced with structured time-off.

9. Protection Against Abuse:
   Locum engagement must not be used as a permanent substitute for substantive recruitment or as a means of exploiting healthcare workers.

10. Integration & Safety: All locum workers must undergo mandatory orientation and integration into their respective clinical or administrative teams. Institutions are required to provide safe 
working environment, adequate call rooms, refreshments during prolonged calls/shifts, and burnout prevention programs.

11. Discipline & Grievance Process: Professional misconduct shall be governed by the regulatory 
council guidelines. Contracts can be terminated by either party with a one-month notice or payment in lieu, and all accrued entitlements must be settled within 14 days of termination. Disputes escalate through institutional mechanisms up to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, and the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment.

12. Monitoring: The Ministry would ensure Institutions do not engage in exploitative staffing practices and violations of this guideline in line with the Nigerian Labour Law.

13. Policy Review and Effective Date:
This policy becomes legally binding on the exact date of approval by the Federal Ministry of 
Health and Social Welfare (FMoH&SW). To ensure its continuous operational relevance, the 
policy mandates a comprehensive evaluation and review within two (2) years of its 
implementation.

The policy is expected to provide a more structured and equitable framework for locum engagement across Nigerian health institutions.

Appreciation to the Hon. Coordinating Minister for Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Mohammad Ali Pate for this approval.

Special appreciation to the Hon. Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr. Iziak Adekunle Salako for his guidance and dictation to seeing this through.

Appreciations are also in order to our distinguished NARDites in the Committee for a job well done. Thank you Dr. Kwarshak Kevin Yakubu, the VP 2 of NARD. Thank you Dr. Shuaibu Ibrahim, the Secretary General of NARD.

NARD is particularly proud of this accomplishments and proves once again what we can achieve when we come together as a team.

NARD remains committed to protecting the dignity, welfare, rights and professional interests of every Nigerian doctor.

It is our hope that the National Council on Health will also give their stamp of approval on this.

Dr. Abdulmajid Yahya Ibrahim
NARD PSS

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. The dispute centers around a video titled “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? | Kerala Story 2 EXPOSED”, which Rathee uploaded in March.

Advocate @SachdevaAmita (Amita Sachdeva) filed a petition alleging that the video contained “false, misleading, and provocative statements” claiming that Hindu deities Lord Ram, Lord Krishna, and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol. She argued this severely hurt the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus.

Following a High Court order to expedite the grievance on July 3, the Central Government's Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) directed Google on July 15 to remove the video within 24 hours.

The petitioner has pushed for a global injunction, pointing out that the video remains accessible globally and via Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) inside India, viewing geo-blocking as “partial compliance”.

Presiding Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma noted that Google has executed what it can under current domestic boundaries, as the broader legal issue regarding global takedown mandates is already pending before a separate Division Bench of the High Court.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

People misunderstand both how Indian IT law functions and how X operates in sovereign jurisdictions.

Code vs. Legal Compliance: An open-source recommendation algorithm simply shows how posts are ranked or flagged in software. It does not override local statutory laws.

Under Indian law, if a platform refuses to comply with an official Section 69A order, its local executives face criminal liability and prison terms, and the platform risks losing its legal "safe harbour" intermediary protection or being banned entirely.

Elon Musk has repeatedly stated on record that X must obey local sovereign laws - "If we have a choice of either our people going to prison or us complying with the laws, we will comply with the laws."

Government takedown requests have never been completely secret:

Both Twitter (pre-Musk) and X have regularly published biannual Transparency Reports listing the number of government legal demands and compliance rates by country.

Making filtering mechanisms visible in code simply adds developer transparency, but it does not change whether the government issues orders or whether X complies with them.

Revealing how an algorithm suppresses or geo-blocks a post does nothing to stop legal enforcement under Indian law, and X will continue complying with sovereign directives to protect its business and staff in the country.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

The news comes as Instagram’s popular news account @Muslim, with over 6.7 million followers, remains blocked in India since May 2025 following a government legal request. The page is visible globally but inaccessible inside India. Founder Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh, speaking February 3 at Web Summit Qatar in Doha, said the ban followed the outlet’s coverage of Palestine: “Because we kept on publishing about Palestine, we’re the only social media account that’s banned in India… they don’t like the fact that we are counteracting western and mainstream power structures.” Meta has cited confidentiality and provided no details on appeal options.

The new Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, notified February 10, tighten platform obligations. Companies must remove content flagged by court or government order within 3 hours, down from 36. The rules also mandate labeling and traceability for AI-generated content, require user disclosure of AI use, and increase liability risks. Critics warn the compressed timeline could drive automated over-removal and significantly expand state control over online speech.

Merritronix is a B2B Electronics System Design & Manufacturing (ESDM) company focused on high-reliability, mission-critical electronics for Defence, Aerospace, Telecom and Industrial applications.

Founded in 1988, the company has evolved from a PCB assembly player into a full-lifecycle electronics manufacturing partner with 37+ years of operating history and an order book of ₹98.06 Cr (June 2026).

Business Model

• Job Work – PCB assembly, soldering and testing using customer-supplied materials.
• Turnkey Manufacturing – End-to-end execution from component sourcing to PCB assembly, system integration, testing and ready-to-deploy products.
• Obsolescence Management – Reverse engineering, obsolete component sourcing and redesign to extend the life of legacy defence platforms.
• Trading Sales – Supply of electronic and electromechanical components from global suppliers to reduce customers' supply-chain risks.

Products & Capabilities

• High-density PCB assemblies (SMT & THT)
• Box-build solutions
• System integration
• Functional testing
• Electronic assemblies for airborne radar systems
• Missile seeker assemblies
• Defence aircraft digital video recorders
• Custom semiconductor solutions
• Reverse engineering & lifecycle extension for legacy defence electronics

Key End Markets

• Aerospace & Defence (97.8% of FY26 revenue)
• Power & Utilities
• Heavy Engineering
• Electrical Engineering
• Industrial Electronics

The company is an approved supplier to Bharat Electronics (BEL) and Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL), while also supplying Honeywell Aerospace and exporting to Europe.

Competitive Strengths

• 86% repeat customer rate, reflecting strong customer relationships.
• High-entry-barrier defence manufacturing business with stringent certifications and long qualification cycles.
• EN9100:2018 certified with discussions underway for NADCAP certification.
• Advanced manufacturing infrastructure including AOI, X-Ray inspection, IPC Class-3 processes and BGA/Micro-BGA capabilities.
• Strong niche in obsolescence engineering, an increasingly important opportunity as ageing defence platforms require lifecycle extension.

Growth Strategy

• Capacity expansion through new Panasonic NPM D3A SMT line and continued automation.
• Move up the value chain from PCB assembly to complete system design, prototyping and manufacturing.
• Increase direct engagement with defence PSUs to improve margins and reduce intermediary dependence.
• Expand into adjacent markets such as UAV electronics, EV power electronics and advanced industrial applications.
• Grow exports and onboard larger global OEM customers.
• Strengthen growth through strategic partnerships.

Recent Business Updates

• Partnered with Analinear Design Technologies to manufacture analog and mixed-signal electronics, expanding opportunities across industrial, automotive, communications and defence.
• Signed an exclusive manufacturing partnership with Stuam Technologies, strengthening its position in defence communications, radar systems and mission-critical electronics.

Why It Stands Out

Merritronix operates in a niche, high-entry-barrier segment where execution quality, certifications and customer trust matter more than scale. As India pushes defence indigenisation and electronics manufacturing, the company is positioning itself to transition from a contract manufacturer to a higher-value integrated systems partner with improving margins and a broader addressable market.

Indian Data Center Legal Investigation Series : Part 1

Data Centers are "critical infrastructure"? Does this statement has legal force?

Here is the full legal investigation of both — this is the core of "No Law" argument.

1. GAZETTE NOTIFICATION 11 OCT 2022 — Infrastructure Tag

What it is:
F. No. 13/1/2017-INF — Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance. Updates Harmonized Master List of Infrastructure Sub-sectors [first created in 2013, updated 2021].

Line inserted: “Data Centre is included in the category of 'Communication' with footnote — Data Centre housed in a dedicated/centralized building for storage and processing of digital data applications with a minimum capacity of 5 MW of IT load”

Statutory Legal Force — VERY LIMITED:

- This is NOT an Act of Parliament. It's an executive notification under executive power.
- Parent authority? No Act defines Harmonized Master List. It's an internal MoF classification for lending.
- What it actually does: Allows data center companies to get easier institutional credit at lower rates, attract foreign investments, ECB eligibility, longer tenure loans, lower risk weights for banks. That's it.

- What it DOES NOT do:
    - Does NOT give power to acquire land
    - Does NOT exempt from Environment Protection Act, 1986 / EIA Notification 2006
    - Does NOT exempt from Forest Conservation Act, Wildlife Protection Act near Kambalakonda
    - Does NOT give right to use water, power, or process citizens' data
    - Does NOT create liability, accountability, transparency 

So legally: It's a banking classification tag, not a data center governance law. You can get cheap loan, but you still need all other laws. Govt is using it as if it's a license — it's not.

2. UNION BUDGET 2026-27 — Tax Holiday Till 2047

What it is — As per PIB:
"Recognising the need to enable critical infrastructure and boost investment in data centres, I propose to provide tax holiday till 2047 to any foreign company that provides cloud services to customers globally by using data centre services from India. It will, however, need to provide services to Indian customers through an Indian reseller entity. I also propose to provide a safe harbour of 15% on cost in case the company providing data centre services from India is a related entity"

Statutory Legal Force — CONDITIONAL:

- Budget Speech = Zero force. Speech on Feb 1 2026 has no law value.
- Force comes ONLY IF Finance Bill 2026 is passed as Finance Act 2026 by Parliament and notified under Income-tax Act.
- Then it's a tax exemption law only — for 21 years [2026-2047].
- Condition: Serve global customers from India DC, Indian customers via reseller. Safe harbour 15% if related party 

What it DOES NOT do:
- Does NOT create Data Center Act
- Does NOT mandate EIA, SIA, Gram Sabha consent
- Does NOT fix liability for surveillance misuse, data breach, or SMART-warfare dual-use
- Does NOT regulate water/power/carbon
- Does NOT give citizens right to audit

Revenue Secretary justification: _"global cloud companies operate data centres across multiple countries, difficult to link revenue to any single facility. Taxing global income could create uncertainty"_ — Means Govt is scared to tax Google/AWS/Microsoft if they use India DC. 

Result: $270B global greenfield data centre investments in 2025 — India wants pie, so offering 21-year zero tax.

Infrastructure Tag + Tax Holiday = Benefits Without Law

- 11 Oct 2022: Infra status — Cheap loans, ECB, FDI
- 1 Feb 2026: Tax holiday till 2047 — Zero tax on global cloud income from Data Centers located in India

What Govt DID NOT Give
- No Data Center Act
- No EIA for 5MW to 1GW expansion
- No Consent law
- No Accountability, No Liability
- No Protection for Land, Water, Power

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. 🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Or believe social media accounts are spreading fake and baseless news?
